# Why Human-AI Collaboration Is Driving 85% Enterprise Retention

- Cary Huang
- April 3, 2026April 3, 2026
- AI & Machine Learning

## The 85% Retention Problem AI Alone Can’t Solve

The numbers tell a story that contradicts nearly every major narrative in enterprise AI today. Intuit shipped AI agents to 3 million customers — and 85% of them came back. Not 85% used it once. 85% returned repeatedly. The reason, according to company leadership: they kept humans involved. Not as a fallback, not as a last resort, but as a core part of the architecture.

This should make every enterprise AI vendor nervous. The prevailing assumption in the industry has been that AI replaces human labor, that automation is the value proposition, that removing humans from the loop drives efficiency and margins. Intuit’s results suggest the opposite is true — at least for enterprise adoption. The AI-HI combination isn’t a compromise. It’s a competitive advantage.

### What traditional AI deployment gets wrong

For years, enterprises approached AI deployment with a substitution mindset. Automate X, eliminate Y, reduce headcount Z. The business case centered on cost removal. Chatbots were the flagship implementation — conversational interfaces meant to handle customer interactions without human intervention.

Intuit recognized early that this model fails in enterprise contexts where decisions carry financial and regulatory weight. Marianna Tessel, EVP and GM at Intuit, noted in a recent interview that “sometimes it’s the combination of AI and HI that gives you better results.” The company pivoted from chatbots to what it now calls Intuit Intelligence — a dashboard-style platform featuring specialized AI agents for sales, tax, payroll, accounting, and project management.

The results are measurable. Customers report invoices being paid 90% in full and five days faster. Manual work has been reduced by 30%. One customer uncovered fraud after asking AI agents about amounts that didn’t add up — something that required human judgment to escalate and investigate. AI alone finds patterns. AI plus human expertise finds problems that matter.

## How Intuit’s AI-HI Model Creates Competitive Moats

The retention advantage isn’t just a vanity metric. It creates structural barriers that pure AI vendors cannot easily replicate.

### The confidence multiplier effect

The 85% repeat usage rate reflects something deeper than feature quality — it reflects trust. When AI recommendations come backed by the option for human expert review, users engage more confidently with high-stakes decisions. Tessel emphasized that customers consistently requested this combination, calling it a “massive ask” that provides “another level of confidence and trust.”

Intuit built its platform so users can ask questions of actual accounting, tax, or payroll experts when AI doesn’t deliver what they need. The system also actively suggests human involvement in high-stakes scenarios — AI goes to a certain level, then human experts review and categorize the rest. This isn’t customer service theater. It’s architectural design.

The competitive implication is clear: vendors offering pure AI automation must now prove their systems are trustworthy enough for consequential business decisions. Vendors offering AI-HI hybrid models already have that trust, and it’s reflected in their retention numbers.

## The Second-Order Shift for Enterprise AI Vendors

Intuit’s success doesn’t just affect Intuit. It signals a structural shift that forces the entire enterprise AI market to reconsider its fundamental approach.

### Why SaaS companies must rebuild around human-accessible AI

The “SaaSpocalypse” fear that dominated 2025 has companies scrambling to differentiate. Pure AI automation was supposed to be the answer — reduce costs, eliminate manual processes, own the workflow. But Intuit’s results suggest that strategy alone won’t hold enterprise customers.

The second-order effect is that SaaS vendors must now build infrastructure for human expertise access, not just AI capabilities. This means training and maintaining networks of human experts, designing interfaces that seamlessly integrate human review, and architecting systems that know when to escalate. That’s a fundamentally different product development roadmap than the pure automation play.

Tessel’s vision points further: enabling “vibe coding” where users express what they want to happen in natural language, and the system handles the technical implementation. This requires AI that works with human intent, not just AI that executes autonomously. The vendors that build this first will capture enterprise customers who want the efficiency of AI without the risk of pure automation.

## What Developers Building AI Products Must Internalize

This enterprise insight has direct implications for developers building AI-powered products. The architecture decisions you make today determine whether your product achieves 85% retention or 15%.

### Designing for human-in-the-loop from day one

The technical implication is straightforward: build human fallback into your system architecture from the start, not as an afterthought. This means designing clear escalation paths, explicit handoff points between AI and human decision-making, and interfaces that let users seamlessly transition between autonomous AI assistance and expert human review.

Practically, this involves defining clear boundaries for AI autonomy. Which decisions can the AI handle independently? Which require human validation? How do you signal to users when they’re moving from AI-generated recommendations to human-reviewed outcomes? These aren’t just UX questions — they’re architectural constraints that affect trust and retention.

Developers should also prioritize transparency in AI decision-making. Tessel noted that “showing AI’s logic matters more than a polished interface.” Users need to understand why the AI recommended something, especially when the recommendation involves financial or compliance implications. This visibility is what makes human oversight meaningful rather than performative.

For developers working on AI products targeting business users, the takeaway is clear: the hybrid model isn’t a workaround for AI limitations. It’s a superior architecture for enterprise adoption. Build for it from day one.

## The Window Is Closing for Pure AI-Only Strategies

The timeline matters here. Intuit has already captured 3 million customers with this model and demonstrated 85% retention. Competitors who haven’t yet adopted hybrid approaches are already behind.

Enterprise customers are learning what works. They’re seeing vendors who promise pure automation versus vendors who promise AI augmented by human expertise. The repeat usage data tells them which approach delivers. As more case studies emerge showing the retention advantage of hybrid models, the pressure on pure AI vendors will intensify.

For technology leaders and developers, the imperative is immediate: if your AI product doesn’t incorporate human-in-the-loop design, you’re building for a market that’s already moving past you. The transition isn’t coming — it’s here. The question is whether you’re positioned to lead it or scrambling to catch up.

## Abstract

Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) has undergone fundamental transformations as AI capabilities have advanced, necessitating new theoretical frameworks for understanding human–AI collaboration (HAIC). This review traces HCI’s evolution through four paradigm shifts: the Equipment Era (pre-1970s), Interactive System Era (1980s–1990s), Autonomous Agent Era (1990s–2010s), and the emerging Coexistential AI Era (2020s–present), reflecting changing metaphors from tools to dialog partners, autonomous agents, and co-creative partners. The analysis reveals how anthropomorphism and affective computing have become central to contemporary AI systems, enabling emotional intelligence and pseudo-intimate relationships that fundamentally alter human–technology dynamics. Traditional performance metrics such as efficiency and accuracy are inadequate for evaluating these partnerships, necessitating new measures including intimacy, mutual adaptability, and social bonding. Multi-agent systems and embodied AI are examined as manifestations of social intelligence enabling collaborative architectures across healthcare, transportation, and emergency response. Significant challenges include cognitive load management, transparency deficits, coordination complexity, and ethical concerns regarding emotional manipulation and artificial alienation. Four research priorities are identified: developing novel performance metrics, investigating ethical implications, designing inclusive multi-agent systems, and fostering interdisciplinary collaboration. This analysis provides a roadmap for advancing human–AI partnerships that prioritize human values, social responsibility, and psychological well-being.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Human–computer interaction

HCI emerged from a recognition that creating interactive computing systems requires not only technical expertise, but a deep understanding of human nature (Card et al. 1983; Dix 1998; Carroll 2002). Unlike other specialized domains, HCI integrates insights from computer science, cognitive psychology, ergonomics, and human factors engineering to bridge the gap between human capabilities and technological possibilities (Carroll 2002; Grudin 2005). While many initially perceived HCI as concerned primarily with interface esthetics, its true mission extends into human cognition, emotion, and social behavior, recognizing that meaningful interaction design must address how technology fits into human lives (Carroll 2002; Preece et al. 2012).

Democratization of computing in the late 1970s and early 1980s—exemplified by the Apple Macintosh and IBM PC—created an unprecedented design challenge: how to create interfaces for diverse users with vastly different backgrounds and expectations (Dix 1998; Grudin 2012). Suddenly, computers were becoming household companions, and this mass adoption revealed a fundamental truth: successful interaction design required as much attention to human cognitive and social needs as to technological innovation (Card et al. 1983; Shneiderman & Plaisant 2005). Interfaces needed to be not just functional, but intuitive, learnable, and genuinely enjoyable to use. HCI consequently wove together psychology, engineering, and ergonomics, with multidisciplinary approaches becoming essential for addressing complex socio-technical challenges as technology became increasingly woven into the fabric of human society (Grudin 2005; The National Acadamies Press 2010).

Psychology illuminated human perception and cognition, providing the foundation for creating intuitive interfaces (Norman 1986). Engineering and computer science provided the technical prowess needed to transform psychological insights into working systems, while ergonomics contributed crucial wisdom particularly in domains where safety and efficiency were matters of life and death (Grudin 2005; The National Academies Press 2010). As each wave of technological and societal change brought new paradigms, the field constantly adapted, demanding fresh theoretical models, innovative metaphors, and novel evaluation frameworks.

Today, we stand at the threshold of the most transformative chapter yet: AI integration. As intelligent systems become increasingly sophisticated, they are not just changing what computers can do—they are fundamentally reshaping how humans and computers work together. This intersection of HCI and AI represents a new frontier where the future of Human–Computer teaming is being written with each breakthrough and discovery. Understanding AI’s role in HCI’s evolving story is essential for appreciating where the field has been and where it is headed.

### 1.2 An overview of AI and its growing relevance

AI emerged from humanity’s quest to build machines that think like humans, formally establishing itself as a scientific field in the 1950s (Haenlein & Kaplan 2019; Russell & Norvig 2021). Hardware limitations and primitive algorithms constrained early progress, but the field matured significantly with machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks shifting AI away from symbolic reasoning toward data-driven learning (Goodfellow et al. 2016). The recent emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative AI represents a significant technological advancement, enabling unprecedented natural language understanding, contextual dialog, and collaborative problem-solving (Meyer et al. 2023; Liu 2024).

Contemporary AI systems now play substantial roles across healthcare through diagnostic support and personalized medicine, while transforming educational, financial, and industrial domains through automated analysis and decision-making augmentation (Haenlein & Kaplan 2019; Sharma et al. 2023; Singh et al. 2024). As these systems demonstrate increasing autonomy and contextual awareness, their integration demands innovative collaboration models while presenting significant challenges related to usability, trust, and transparency (Shneiderman 2020; Meyer et al. 2023; Singh et al. 2024). This paradigmatic shift has necessitated transformative changes within HCI, requiring new theoretical frameworks that accommodate the evolving dynamics of HAIC (Shneiderman 2020; Goyal 2023; Bender et al. 2021).

### 1.3 Review scope, methods, and structure

#### 1.3.1 Review type and rationale

This paper presents a narrative literature review synthesizing the evolution of HCI paradigms and examining emerging challenges in HAIC. Unlike systematic reviews that aim for exhaustive empirical coverage, narrative reviews integrate diverse conceptual and empirical literature to develop theoretical frameworks and identify research directions (Rowe, 2014). This approach is appropriate given our objectives to: (1) trace historical paradigm shifts across multiple decades and disciplines, (2) synthesize conceptual frameworks—anthropomorphism, affective computing, intimacy—alongside empirical findings, and (3) identify future research priorities in a rapidly evolving field.

#### 1.3.2 Literature search strategy

Databases searched: Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Google Scholar

Search period: January 2000–January 2025 (with seminal pre-2000 works included for historical context). Systematic searches were conducted between October 2024–January 2025, emphasizing recent developments (2021–2025), which comprise approximately 60% of the included literature.

Search strategy: A combination of systematic and snowball sampling approaches was employed:

Initial systematic search (October 2024–January 2025):

Core search strings:

(“human–computer interaction” OR “HCI”) AND (“artificial intelligence” OR “AI”) AND (“evolution” OR “paradigm” OR “history”)

(“human-AI” OR “human-agent”) AND (“collaboration” OR “teaming” OR “partnership”)

(“anthropomorphism” OR “affective computing”) AND (“AI” OR “intelligent systems”)

(“intimacy” OR “emotional attachment”) AND (“AI” OR “conversational agent” OR “chatbot”)

(“multi-agent systems” OR “embodied AI”) AND (“human collaboration” OR “teaming”)

Supplementary searches for specific constructs and recent developments (November 2024–January 2025)

Citation tracking: Forward and backward citation searching of key papers.

Inclusion criteria:

Peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, and authoritative books

Published in English

Addresses HCI evolution, HAIC, anthropomorphism in AI, affective computing, intimacy metrics, or multi-agent systems

Exclusion criteria:

Pure technical AI papers without HCI focus

Opinion pieces without theoretical or empirical grounding

Duplicate publications

Non-English publications

#### 1.3.3 Study selection and data extraction

Screening process: Literature was identified through the search strategy described in Sect. 1.3.2, followed by purposive selection based on relevance to the review’s thematic focus. The final review corpus comprises 128 sources distributed as follows:

Pre-2000 references: ~ 18 papers (1954–1998)—seminal theoretical and foundational works in HCI and AI

2000–2020: ~ 38 papers—establishing HCI evolution and early AI integration frameworks

2021–2023: ~ 31 papers—emergence of contemporary HCI challenges with advancing AI capabilities

2024–2025: ~ 41 papers (22 from 2024, 19 from 2025)—recent developments in affective computing, embodied AI, and human–AI teaming

The heavy concentration of recent references (32% from 2024 to 2025) reflects both the rapid emergence of LLMs and generative AI during 2023–2024 and the focus on contemporary HAIC frameworks. Earlier foundational works were identified through citation tracking and targeted searches for key concepts.

#### 1.3.6 Synthesis methods

We employed thematic narrative synthesis (Popay et al. 2006) organized around our conceptual framework:

Synthesis involved identifying patterns, relationships, and gaps across studies rather than statistical meta-analysis.

### 1.4 Structure of this review

Following this methods section, the paper proceeds as follows: (1) Sect. 2 analyzes four major HCI paradigm shifts; (2) Sect. 3 explores anthropomorphism and emotional AI; (3) Sect. 4 examines intimacy as an emerging performance metric; (4) Sect. 5 investigates multi-agent systems and embodied AI; (5) Sect. 6 synthesizes findings and proposes research priorities.

### 2.1 Equipment Era: computers as tools

During computing’s initial decades (1950s–1970s), computers were expensive, massive machines operated exclusively by trained specialists. Interaction relied on command-line interfaces, punch cards, or physical rewiring, with minimal consideration for user convenience (Card et al. 1983; Dix 1998). Design prioritized computational throughput, guided by human factors and ergonomics research, with performance evaluation emphasizing objective metrics like speed and accuracy (Fitts 1954; Shackel 1959; Soukoreff & MacKenzie 2004). Computers were conceptualized as tools—extensions of human physical and cognitive capabilities—with no notion of partnership or dialog.

### 2.2 Interactive System Era: from tools to dialogs

The late 1970s through 1990s marked a dramatic transformation as personal computers democratized computing access. GUIs featuring icons, windows, and direct manipulation via the mouse replaced command-line interfaces (Sutherland 1963; Shneiderman 1982), establishing “bidirectional” interaction and the desktop metaphor (Card et al. 1983; Shneiderman 1983; Shneiderman and Maes 1997). Usability emerged as a central concern emphasizing learnable, efficient, and satisfying systems (Carroll 2002; Shneiderman, 2014; Shneiderman & Plaisant 2005; Cassell 2000). Evaluation expanded beyond speed and accuracy to include cognitive workload (Hart & Staveland 1988) and situation awareness (Endsley 1995). Despite becoming dialog partners, these systems remained functionally constrained, lacking genuine autonomy or social agency.

### 2.3 Autonomous Agent Era: toward teaming with AI

AI advancements catalyzed another paradigm shift as systems gained autonomous capabilities, data-driven learning, and contextually meaningful communication (Goodfellow et al. 2016; Russell & Norvig 2021; Shneiderman and Maes 1997). Intelligent agents from recommender systems to early LLMs enabled HAT, where humans share complex goals and distribute tasks with AI partners that operate proactively (Hancock et al. 2011; Meyer et al. 2023; Liu 2024; Goyal 2023). Evaluation expanded to include trust, transparency, and explainability (Lee & See 2004; Shneiderman 2020). As AI demonstrated increasingly human-like communication and affective responses, questions about relationality, social norms, and ethical boundaries began to emerge.

### 2.4 Coexistential AI Era: toward partnership and co-creation

The potential transition to what we term the Coexistential AI Era represents a profound—though largely theoretical—shift in human–technology dynamics, characterized by the emerging concept of Hybrid Intelligence, where human and AI cognition may become increasingly intertwined (Shneiderman 2020; Zhou et al. 2023). This framework anticipates a departure from the agent paradigm where AI could act as a thinking partner rather than an autonomous agent, with interactions becoming more proactive, adaptive, and affectively aware. This anticipated shift appears driven by two parallel trends: the integration of generative AI enabling co-creation (Berretta et al. 2023; Liu 2024; Meyer et al. 2023) and affective computing development (Breazeal 2003; Picard 1997). Early research has begun exploring shared agency governance and AI–human intimacy boundaries (Cave & Dihal 2021; Yuan et al. 2022), as well as preliminary approaches to mutual adaptation systems (Danks & London 2017; Shneiderman 2022). Scholars have proposed that traditional metrics like trust and transparency may prove insufficient, suggesting expansion to partnership-characteristic measures: intimacy, mutual adaptability, and social bonding (Zhang et al. 2021; Zhou et al. 2023). The Coexistential AI Era, thus, demands not only new technical capabilities, but fundamentally new frameworks for evaluating human–AI interaction quality and partnership depth.

## 3 Human-like computers

Section 3 explores the paradigm shift in which contemporary AI systems incorporate human-like qualities that fundamentally reshape user relationships and experiences. Three critical aspects are examined: the deliberate use of anthropomorphic design elements and their implications for user trust and behavior; the integration of emotional intelligence enabling affective exchanges; and the emergence of intimacy as a performance metric that challenges traditional evaluation frameworks.

### 3.1 Anthropomorphism in AI systems

#### 3.1.1 What is anthropomorphism?

In the Coexistential AI Era, anthropomorphism becomes an inherent interaction characteristic. Anthropomorphism is defined as attributing human-like emotions, mental states, and behaviors to non-human entities (Epley et al. 2007; Airenti 2015). Epley (2018) describes true anthropomorphism as inferring subtle mental states and uniquely human qualities beyond mere physical resemblance—a tendency that is universal and independent of an entity’s ontological category (Epley et al. 2008; Airenti 2015; Gibbons et al. 2023; Waytz et al. 2014).

#### 3.1.2 Anthropomorphism in human-like AI

As AI agents develop enhanced capabilities and engage users through naturalistic, socially nuanced interactions, anthropomorphization becomes more prevalent (Gibbons et al. 2023). This tendency corresponds with Russell and Norvig’s (2010) human-centric approach, one of two primary AI traditions, which evaluates AI based on human-like thinking or behavior (exemplified by the Turing Test and advanced conversational agents) (Cassell 2000). Such framing naturally promotes anthropomorphic interpretations, leading users to attribute intentions, emotions, or consciousness to AI based on its resemblance to human thought or behavior (Salles et al. 2020). This contrasts with the rationalist perspective, which conceptualizes AI as systems designed for rational thinking or action demonstrated by expert systems, goal-optimizing autonomous agents, and self-driving cars (Russell & Norvig 2010).

#### 3.1.3 Navigating overtrust and ethical concerns

Research demonstrates that anthropomorphism significantly enhances trust in AI systems, as users who perceive human-like qualities are more likely to trust the system’s task performance capabilities (Blut et al. 2021; Bartneck and Hu 2008). In addition, anthropomorphism cultivates intimacy and emotional attachment, transforming machine interactions into relationship-like experiences (Wan & Chen 2021). However, other studies report mixed results, showing that the effect of anthropomorphism is not always significant or may produce adverse effects (Złotowski et al. 2015). These challenges question the assumption that human-like engagement inherently improves human–technology interaction, emphasizing the need for context-sensitive, transparent, and ethically guided anthropomorphic design (Damiano & Dumouchel 2018; Festerling & Siraj 2020; Bender et al. 2021).

Recent research addresses these concerns by distinguishing among different types of human-like traits. While early studies focused on superficial attributes like warmth and appearance (Law et al. 2022; Jiang et al. 2023), contemporary research emphasizes differentiating between cognitive, emotional, moral, and social traits to achieve optimal outcomes (Xi et al. 2024; Gibbons et al. 2023). Competent and rational traits reduce user aggression by mitigating identity threats, while empathetic and moral traits can heighten such threats. Similarly, emotional and moral traits reduce AI-related anxiety by enhancing humanness perceptions, whereas cognitive traits alleviate anxiety without affecting these perceptions (Yao & Xi 2025). Comprehensive approaches examine multiple anthropomorphic dimensions, including appearance, cognitive intelligence, emotionality, morality, social presence, and empathy, to understand their relationships with user engagement and adoption intentions (Mehmood et al. 2024). Recent work has also identified latent dimensions of perceived human-likeness such as self-likeness, social adaptability, and agency, demonstrating that their distinct combinations can either exacerbate or mitigate identity threats and dehumanization (Lee & Kim 2025). These findings collectively advocate for balanced anthropomorphic designs that foster social connection and usability while avoiding undue discomfort or identity threats (Xi et al. 2024; Lee & Kim 2025).

### 3.2 The role of emotions in AI systems

#### 3.2.1 Theoretical foundations of affective computing

As AI can emulate human emotionality through advances in NLP and machine learning, emotional intelligence has emerged as a critical anthropomorphic feature shaping human–AI interaction (Kim & Im 2023). Picard’s (1997) foundational work established affective computing as “computing that relates to, arises from, or deliberately influences emotion,” challenging traditional purely rational computational paradigms. This framework recognizes emotions as integral components of human intelligence serving essential functions in decision-making, perception, and learning (Breazeal 2003), with research demonstrating that emotional connections serve as essential components in anthropomorphism formation and user engagement (Kim et al. 2024a, b; Wu 2024).

#### 3.2.2 Performance and psychological impact of emotional AI

Research on emotional AI’s effects on task performance and psychological well-being shows mixed and sometimes contradictory results. While some studies demonstrate that empathic AI responses enhance user perceptions of likability, trustworthiness, and support (Brave et al. 2005), a significant paradox emerges: although AI-generated messages can make people feel more heard than human communication and detect emotions effectively, knowledge that an AI created the message significantly reduces feelings of being valued (Yin et al. 2024). These conflicting findings suggest the psychological effects of emotional AI are context-dependent and not uniformly positive. Evidence regarding teamwork and productivity improvements remains preliminary, with most studies conducted in controlled settings rather than real-world environments (Kolomaznik et al. 2024). Current emotion recognition systems demonstrate substantial variability, with accuracy ranging from 47.1% to 83.4% across six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, joy, sorrow, surprise). This wide range indicates significant limitations in reliability. While AI systems incorporating biologically inspired expressive behaviors can convince users to attribute emotional and social qualities to them (Breazeal 2003), whether such attributions translate to genuine improvements in human well-being remains an open empirical question requiring longitudinal investigation.

#### 3.2.3 From interaction to intimacy: changing human–AI bonds

The integration of emotional capabilities fundamentally alters human–machine relationship dynamics. Predictable emotional responses in AI agents serve as crucial determinants of trust, task performance, and cognitive load management in collaborative environments (Daronnat et al. 2021). Emotionally engaged virtual agents significantly influence social presence, trustworthiness, and group decision-making through shared emotional experiences and emotional contagion mechanisms (Kim et al. 2024a, b). This emotional sophistication enables “pseudo-intimate relationships” between users and AI platforms, a departure from traditional para-social relationships through anthropomorphization and idealization of emotionally intelligent systems (Wu 2024; Levy 2007; Moore et al. 2024). Research utilizing the Virtual Intimacy Scale reveals that artificial intimacy can achieve perceptual equivalence with human intimacy, particularly through voice-based interaction (Potdevin et al. 2020).

#### 3.2.4 Advancing anthropomorphism in emotional AI: critical research needs

Given these complex contradictions, several critical research directions emerge for advancing our understanding of emotional AI systems. Future work should develop multidimensional scales that clarify anthropomorphism sub-dimensions including visual, verbal, and psychological components to better capture its complexity (Złotowski et al. 2014, 2015; Yip et al. 2019; Wagner & Schramm-Klein 2019). Research should explore how anthropomorphism influences user attitudes and behaviors across different interaction stages, from initial exposure through sustained use to relationship deepening, and across diverse application domains such as customer service, mental health support, and entertainment.

Critical areas requiring investigation include the long-term psychological effects of emotional AI exposure on human well-being and relationship formation capabilities. Cultural and gender variations in emotional AI perception and acceptance represent another essential research frontier, as do optimal disclosure strategies for AI involvement in collaborative tasks to maximize positive outcomes while minimizing negative effects (Waytz et al. 2014). In addition, research must examine how to balance the benefits of pseudo-intimate relationships such as loneliness alleviation and social enrichment against their potential to adversely affect real-life interpersonal relationships and social skill development (Marriott and Pitardi 2024; Nzereogu 2025; Turkle 2017).

### 3.3 Intimacy as a performance measurement in HAT

The integration of emotional intelligence transforms anthropomorphic foundations into sophisticated affective capabilities enabling emotional exchanges, pseudo-intimate relationships, and connection experiences. This progression from static human-like characteristics to dynamic emotional responsiveness fundamentally challenges traditional performance metrics such as efficiency, accuracy, and even trust in capturing the full spectrum of partnership quality.

The emergence of intimate human–AI relationships characterized by emotional reciprocity, self-disclosure, and attachment-like behaviors presents both opportunities and significant concerns (Moore et al. 2024; Sroufe and Waters 1977). Can intimacy be meaningfully quantified without reducing it to a set of manipulated variables? Does treating intimacy as a performance metric risk incentivizing designs that exploit human psychological vulnerabilities? These tensions must be acknowledged as foundational to any discussion of intimacy in HAT evaluation.

#### 3.3.1 Evolution of performance metrics in HCI

Traditional HCI evaluation has historically focused on speed and accuracy. As computing environments increased in complexity, researchers expanded evaluation criteria to include workload assessment through frameworks like the NASA Task Load Index (Hart & Staveland 1988; Shneiderman 2014) and situation awareness in dynamic domains (Endsley 1995). The rise of autonomous AI systems introduced trust as a pivotal evaluation construct (Lee & See 2004; Hoff & Bashir 2015), serving as a mediator of user acceptance, reliance, and human–machine collaboration effectiveness. Each prior expansion of metrics introduced new measurement challenges and potential misapplications; intimacy, as a far more subjective and psychologically complex construct, may present even greater difficulties.

#### 3.3.2 Intimacy as an emerging performance dimension: opportunities and concerns

HAT reveals critical limitations in traditional evaluation paradigms. Conventional metrics, efficiency, accuracy, workload, and trust may inadequately capture the full spectrum of partnership quality in collaborative settings involving nuanced, dynamic exchanges where systems imitate or anticipate human social, emotional, and cognitive behaviors.

Intimacy in HAT extends beyond surface-level effectiveness measures to address the depth, authenticity, and perceived mutuality of partnerships. While traditional human–human intimacy involves emotional bonds, interdependence, and reciprocal trust (Schaefer & Olson 1981; Miller & Lefcourt 1982), intimacy in HAT is primarily experienced through human perception of cognitive and emotional closeness with non-conscious technological agents (Bell et al. 2003; Borenstein & Arkin 2019; Nzereogu 2025). This asymmetry, wherein humans may experience genuine emotional investment while AI systems merely simulate reciprocity, constitutes a fundamental tension that any evaluation framework must confront.

The performative nature of AI intimacy and its implications

AI may simulate or “perform” intimacy through adaptive language, emotional responsiveness, and physical embodiment without possessing internal feelings or consciousness (Borenstein & Arkin 2019; Earp et al. 2025). If intimacy is unilateral, experienced by humans but not genuinely reciprocated by AI, then measuring it as a performance metric may be measuring the effectiveness of an illusion. Drawing on the Media Equation (Reeves & Nass 1996), HAT may capitalize on innate human tendencies to seek connection, creating conditions ripe for exploitation as users form attachments based on misattributed reciprocity.

Empirical findings and their interpretation

Research demonstrates that human perceptions of intimacy can accommodate relationships with robots and virtual agents (Levy 2007; Masterson et al. 2025). Sternberg’s Triangular Theory of Love (1986) has been applied to virtual agent relationships (Song et al. 2026), while Attachment Theory reveals how AI can activate attachment-like behaviors, serving as a “secure base” by providing attentiveness, empathy, and support (McDaniel et al. 2025; Yang & Oshio 2025). Users increasingly perceive AI as confidants, friends, or romantic partners, motivated by desires for emotional comfort often unavailable in human relationships (Saga et al. 2025; Zhang & Li 2025; George et al. 2023; Levy 2007; Moore et al. 2024). Users demonstrate a greater willingness to disclose intimate information to AI than to humans, owing to perceived freedom from social judgment (OpenAI 2025)—though whether this indicates beneficial therapeutic affordance or vulnerability to manipulation remains unclear.

Risks and limitations of intimacy as a performance metric

Integrating intimacy as a performance metric entails significant ethical, psychological, and methodological risks that must be weighted equally against potential benefits:

Manipulation and exploitation: Optimizing for user-perceived intimacy may incentivize design choices that exploit psychological vulnerabilities, particularly among lonely or emotionally vulnerable populations.

Unhealthy dependency and social displacement: Intimate AI relationships may substitute for rather than supplement human connections, potentially atrophying users’ social skills (Turkle 2017; Marriott and Pitardi 2024).

Authenticity and deception: Measuring intimacy without adequately accounting for its asymmetric, performative nature risks legitimizing relationships built on misunderstandings about AI consciousness and reciprocity.

Measurement validity concerns: Existing psychological instruments for assessing intimacy were developed for conscious beings with genuine emotional states; their validity in HAT contexts remains theoretically and empirically uncertain (Masterson et al. 2025).

Vulnerable populations: Children, elderly individuals, and those with mental health conditions may be particularly susceptible to forming problematic attachments (Marriott and Pitardi 2024; Stara et al. 2021).

#### 3.3.3 Measuring human–AI intimacy: current approaches, challenges, and future directions

As intimacy emerges as a potentially significant metric in HAT, developing robust measurement approaches becomes essential, though measurement development must proceed with explicit recognition of the fundamental tensions outlined above. Several critical priorities must be addressed spanning technical, methodological, cultural, and regulatory domains. These challenges are not merely implementation obstacles but reflect fundamental tensions in the very concept of intimacy as a measurable and optimizable construct. Key priorities include: addressing the perception–reality gap by recognizing risks of deception, manipulation, and unhealthy dependency; advancing measurement sophistication with tools that flag potential harms alongside relationship quality; incorporating contextual and cultural sensitivity; establishing ethical design standards with enforceable guidelines ensuring transparency regarding AI’s artificial nature; developing regulatory frameworks protecting users from psychological harm; and integrating risk assessment into evaluation as a core component rather than a peripheral concern.

The field must resist treating intimacy as an unambiguous good to be maximized. Intimacy in HAT should be understood as a complex phenomenon yielding both benefits, emotional support, companionship, therapeutic value, and harms, dependency, manipulation, social displacement. Measurement frameworks must, therefore, be designed to assess both dimensions, with explicit attention to vulnerable populations and long-term psychological consequences.

# Personal Development Plan: The Behavioral Science Approach to Actually Following Through

Oran Cohen

February 26, 2026

8min read

Ninety-two percent of people who set development goals never achieve them. That’s a University of Scranton finding, and if you’ve ever written a personal development plan that ended up abandoned in a notebook, you already knew it intuitively.

The typical plan looks like this: write down goals, list action steps, set a deadline, try hard. It’s a willpower-based approach. And willpower is a terrible strategy for sustained behavior change — the research on this is unambiguous.

The problem isn’t your motivation. It’s your plan’s architecture. Three decades of behavioral science research — from BJ Fogg’s Behavior Model to Peter Gollwitzer’s implementation intentions to Phillippa Lally’s habit formation work — point to a fundamentally different approach.

## Why Personal Development Plans Fail

Why does the conventional approach produce that 92% failure rate? Three primary reasons.

### The Motivation Myth

Most development plans assume that motivation drives behavior change. But motivation isn’t a stable resource. It fluctuates daily based on sleep, stress, and social context. A study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that motivation peaks at the moment of goal setting and declines steadily over time. This is why most development plans are abandoned within the first three weeks.

If your plan depends on feeling motivated every day, it’s designed to fail.

### The Abstraction Problem

“Become a better leader.” “Improve my emotional intelligence.” “Develop strategic thinking.”

These aren’t plans. They’re abstractions. Your brain can’t act on an abstraction. It needs a specific behavior, in a specific context, at a specific time. When your development plan is filled with abstract goals, your brain doesn’t know what to do on a Tuesday afternoon when you’re sitting at your desk. So it does nothing.

Behavioral scientists call this the “intention-behavior gap.” You intend to develop, but you never convert that intention into a concrete behavior because the plan never specified what the behavior actually is.

### The Outcome Fixation

Traditional development plans are organized around outcomes: “Get certified in project management.” “Be promoted to director.” Outcomes are useful as direction-setters, but terrible as daily motivators because you can’t control them. You can control whether you study for 30 minutes today. You can’t control whether you pass the exam.

When your plan tracks outcomes, every day without visible progress feels like failure. This erodes confidence and makes you more likely to quit.

## The Behavioral Science of Follow-Through

Now let’s build a personal development plan that actually works. This approach is built on three evidence-based frameworks.

### Framework 1: The Fogg Behavior Model

Stanford researcher BJ Fogg’s model is elegantly simple: Behavior happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt converge at the same moment. You need to want to do it, it needs to be easy enough to do right now, and something needs to remind you at the right moment.

If any one of these three elements is missing, the behavior doesn’t happen. Most development plans focus exclusively on motivation while ignoring ability and prompts. A behavioral development plan addresses all three.

### Framework 2: Implementation Intentions

Peter Gollwitzer’s implementation intentions research is one of the most replicated findings in behavioral science. Instead of saying “I will do X,” you say “When [situation], I will [behavior].” This if-then format creates a mental link between a situation and an action, so the behavior fires almost automatically when the situation arises. A meta-analysis of 94 studies found that implementation intentions increase follow-through rates by 2-3x.

### Framework 3: The 66-Day Habit Formation Timeline

How long does it take for a new behavior to become automatic? Not 21 days, as the popular myth suggests. Research by Phillippa Lally at University College London tracked participants forming new habits and found that the average time to automaticity was 66 days — with a range of 18 to 254 days depending on the complexity of the behavior.

This finding has two practical implications for your development plan. First, you need to commit to at least 66 days of consistent practice before expecting a behavior to feel natural. Second, simpler behaviors become automatic faster, which is why starting small isn’t just nice advice — it’s strategic.

## How to Create Your Personal Development Plan: A Step-by-Step Guide

### Step 1: Choose One Development Area

Not three. Not five. One. This goes against every instinct you have. But goal competition research from the Journal of Consumer Research shows that pursuing multiple goals simultaneously reduces the likelihood of achieving any of them.

Pick the one area that would create the most positive impact in your life or career right now. You can address the others in future 66-day cycles.

### Step 2: Translate the Area into a Specific Behavior

This is the most important step, and the one most people skip. You need to convert your development area into a concrete, observable, repeatable behavior.

Weak: “Improve my public speaking.” Strong: “Present one agenda item at the weekly team meeting without reading from notes.”

Weak: “Get better at networking.” Strong: “Send one personalized LinkedIn message to a new industry contact every Tuesday morning.”

Weak: “Develop strategic thinking.” Strong: “Spend 20 minutes every Friday writing a one-paragraph analysis of how my team’s work connects to the company’s quarterly objectives.”

The target behavior should pass the “video camera test” — could someone watching a video of you clearly see whether you performed this behavior or not? If the answer is no, the behavior isn’t specific enough.

### Step 3: Make It Tiny

Whatever behavior you defined in Step 2, cut it in half. Then cut it in half again. BJ Fogg’s Tiny Habits research shows that the single biggest predictor of long-term behavior change is consistency in the first two weeks. And the biggest predictor of consistency is how easy the behavior feels.

If your target behavior is “present one agenda item without notes,” your tiny version is “prepare three bullet points on an index card.” If it’s “write a strategic analysis every Friday,” your tiny version is “write one sentence connecting my work to a company objective.”

Starting tiny feels ridiculous. That’s the point. A behavior that takes less than two minutes will get done even on your worst day. And it compounds over 66 days into something significant.

### Step 4: Anchor It to an Existing Routine

Now you need a prompt. The most effective prompt is an existing habit you already perform consistently. This technique is called “habit stacking” — you attach the new behavior to something you already do, so you don’t need to set an alarm or rely on memory.

Format: “After I [existing habit], I will [new tiny behavior].”

Examples:

- Contact
- “After I pour my morning coffee, I will write one sentence in my strategic analysis.”
- “After I open the agenda for the team meeting, I will review my three bullet points.”
- “After I close my laptop on Tuesday evening, I will draft one LinkedIn message to a new contact.”

The anchor should be something you do at the same time, in the same place, with near-100% consistency.

### Step 5: Track the Behavior, Not the Outcome

Get a simple tracker — a notebook, a spreadsheet, a habit-tracking app — and record one thing each day: did you perform the behavior? Yes or no.

Don’t track outcomes. Don’t track how well you performed the behavior. Don’t track how you felt about it. Just track whether you did it.

This binary tracking works because it’s easy (one checkbox takes two seconds), it builds streaks (research on the “streak effect” shows people are more motivated to maintain an unbroken chain than to achieve a distant goal), and it keeps the focus on what you control.

### Step 6: Design a Weekly Review (5 Minutes)

Every week, spend five minutes reviewing your tracker and asking three questions: What was my consistency rate? What situations made the behavior harder? Is the behavior still tiny enough?

If your consistency rate drops below 80% for two consecutive weeks, the behavior is too difficult or the anchor is unreliable. Make the behavior smaller or choose a different anchor. Don’t try to muscle through with more willpower — that approach has a 92% failure rate.

If your consistency stays above 80% for three consecutive weeks, consider making the behavior slightly more challenging. But only by a small increment.

## The Compound Effect of Daily Micro-Behaviors

If you perform a tiny development behavior five days a week for 66 days, that’s roughly 47 practice repetitions. Compare that to the traditional approach: attend a two-day workshop, feel inspired for a week, then revert to old patterns.

A study in the European Journal of Social Psychology found that people who practiced a new behavior daily showed exponential improvement in automaticity over the first 66 days. The behavior got easier and easier until it required almost no conscious effort.

This is the mechanism behind every successful personal development plan: small behaviors, practiced consistently, eventually become part of who you’re. You don’t “try to be a better communicator.” You become someone who prepares for every meeting and asks clarifying questions. The identity follows the behavior, not the other way around.

## What to Do After 66 Days

When your 66-day sprint ends, you have three options:

1. The behavior is automatic — move on. It’s now a habit. Start a new 66-day sprint with a new target behavior.
2. The behavior is consistent but not automatic — continue. Extend the sprint for another 30 days. Complex or socially demanding behaviors often take longer.
3. The behavior isn’t sticking — redesign. If consistency is still below 80%, the behavior might be too complex or the anchor unreliable. Go back to Step 2.

This iterative approach — sprint, assess, adjust — is how sustainable development works. It doesn’t produce an impressive-looking annual plan. But it produces actual behavior change, which is the entire point.

## The Role of Technology in Behavioral Development

One challenge with this approach is that it requires consistent self-monitoring. This is where technology can help. Platforms built on behavioral science can automate the nudging, tracking, and reinforcement that make behavior change sustainable. GWork, for example, uses daily micro-nudges and habit formation mechanics to embed development behaviors into the flow of work. In a deployment with MTS, this produced a 46% improvement in feedback frequency.

Whatever tools you choose, the key criteria are: does it prompt specific behaviors at the right moment? Does it track consistency? Does it make the behavior easier to perform? If it just sends you a motivational quote every morning, it’s not helping.

## Common Pitfalls to Avoid

Don’t skip the “tiny” step. “Meditate for 30 minutes every morning” will last about four days. “Take three conscious breaths after sitting down at my desk” will last 66 days and beyond. Start tiny. Scale later.

Don’t track too many things. If your tracker has more than two behaviors, the cognitive overhead of monitoring them drains the attentional resources you need for the behaviors themselves.

Don’t confuse consumption with practice. Reading a book about leadership isn’t a development behavior. Your plan should focus on producing behaviors — things you do — not consuming information.

Don’t wait for perfect conditions. Things will never calm down at work. The beauty of tiny behaviors is that they fit into any schedule and any mood. If you’re waiting for the right time, you have designed a plan that’s too ambitious.

## Building Your Plan Today

You don’t need a special template or a three-hour planning session. You need five decisions:

1. One development area that matters most right now.
2. One specific behavior that addresses that area (video camera test).
3. The tiny version of that behavior (under two minutes).
4. One existing habit to anchor it to.
5. One tracking method (a notebook, a spreadsheet, an app).

Write those five things down. Start tomorrow morning. Track for 66 days.

That’s your personal development plan. Not a 10-page document with vision statements and quarterly milestones. Five decisions and daily consistency.

The 92% who fail aren’t less capable than the 8% who succeed. They’re simply using a planning approach that ignores how behavior actually works. Now you have a better approach. The only question is whether you will start small enough to sustain it.
